text: A platform team maintains a shared coding standards document that successfully enforces consistent patterns for most of the team. A newly hired engineer joins and reports that Claude Code never applies the team's error-handling conventions or import ordering rules, even though these are documented and other engineers confirm the rules work for them. The new engineer cloned the repository the same way as everyone else. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The team's `CLAUDE.md` file exceeds the maximum token limit and is being silently truncated for new sessions
Claude Code requires each developer to manually run `/memory` on first use before any `CLAUDE.md` file takes effect
The new engineer needs to regenerate an API key before project-level configuration files can be loaded
The conventions were accidentally placed in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on individual machines rather than in the project-level `.claude/CLAUDE.md` or root `CLAUDE.md` that is checked into version control
correct_answer: The conventions were accidentally placed in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on individual machines rather than in the project-level `.claude/CLAUDE.md` or root `CLAUDE.md` that is checked into version control
explanation: User-level `CLAUDE.md` files (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`) apply only to that individual user and are never shared via version control, unlike project-level (`.claude/CLAUDE.md` or root `CLAUDE.md`) files which are committed and shared with the whole team (option D). If the conventions lived in user-level files instead of the project-level file, existing teammates who had local copies would see consistent behavior while a new engineer cloning the repo would not receive those instructions. The other options (token truncation, a required `/memory` initialization step, or API key gating) are not how Claude Code's configuration hierarchy works.

text: Your team built a `/analyze-deps` skill that performs deep dependency graph analysis across a large monorepo, often producing thousands of lines of exploratory output (file scans, import traces, version conflict logs) before summarizing findings. Developers report that after running this skill, the main conversation becomes so cluttered with exploration detail that Claude's subsequent responses become slower and less focused. Which `SKILL.md` frontmatter configuration best addresses this issue?
options: Set `allowed-tools` to restrict the skill to read-only file operations, preventing it from writing exploratory logs
Set `context: fork` so the skill executes in an isolated sub-agent context, keeping only the final summary in the main conversation
Set `argument-hint` to require developers to specify a narrower dependency scope before the skill runs
Move the skill from `.claude/skills/` to `.claude/commands/` so it runs as a lightweight slash command instead
correct_answer: Set `context: fork` so the skill executes in an isolated sub-agent context, keeping only the final summary in the main conversation
explanation: The `context: fork` frontmatter option (option B) runs a skill in an isolated sub-agent context specifically to prevent verbose or exploratory skill output from polluting the main conversation. This is the documented pattern for skills that produce large amounts of intermediate output (like codebase analysis) where only the final summary is relevant to the ongoing session. Restricting `allowed-tools` (option A) controls which tools the skill can invoke but doesn't address context pollution from legitimate read operations. `argument-hint` (option C) only helps prompt for required parameters, not isolate output. Moving the skill to `.claude/commands/` (option D) doesn't isolate output.

text: Your codebase has Terraform infrastructure files scattered across `infra/aws/`, `infra/gcp/`, and `modules/shared-infra/`, and your team wants Claude Code to always apply strict Terraform naming and tagging conventions whenever any `.tf` file is being edited, regardless of which directory it lives in. You are deciding between creating directory-level `CLAUDE.md` files in each Terraform directory versus a single rule file with path-based scoping. Which approach is most maintainable and why?
options: Create three separate directory-level `CLAUDE.md` files, one in each Terraform directory, since directory-level files are the only way to scope conventions in Claude Code
Add the Terraform conventions to the root `CLAUDE.md` so they are always loaded for every session regardless of file type
Create a single file in `.claude/rules/` with YAML frontmatter specifying `paths: ["**/*.tf"]`, so the convention loads automatically for any matching file regardless of its directory location
Create a custom slash command `/terraform-check` that developers must manually invoke before editing any `.tf` file
correct_answer: Create a single file in `.claude/rules/` with YAML frontmatter specifying `paths: ["**/*.tf"]`, so the convention loads automatically for any matching file regardless of its directory location
explanation: Path-specific rules in `.claude/rules/` use glob patterns in YAML frontmatter to conditionally load conventions based on file type or pattern, independent of directory structure (option C). This is the recommended approach when conventions must apply to files spread across multiple directories (like Terraform files in `aws/`, `gcp/`, and `shared-infra/`), since a single glob pattern like `**/*.tf` covers all of them without duplicating content across multiple directory-level `CLAUDE.md` files. Maintaining three separate directory-level `CLAUDE.md` files (option A) duplicates effort and risks drift between copies. Adding the rules to root `CLAUDE.md` (option B) loads them for every file type unnecessarily, wasting context on non-Terraform work. A manual slash command (option D) relies on developers remembering to invoke it rather than automatic, conditional application.

text: Your team is evaluating two upcoming tasks for Claude Code. Task A: migrate the application's HTTP client library from `axios` to `fetch` across roughly 50 files, where the migration pattern is well-documented and mechanical but touches many files. Task B: fix a null pointer exception in a single checkout validation function, with a clear stack trace pointing to the exact line. How should your team approach each task?
options: Use plan mode for Task A to scope the mechanical changes across all 50 files and validate the approach before execution; use direct execution for Task B since it is a well-understood, single-file fix
Use direct execution for both tasks since Claude Code only needs plan mode for tasks involving genuine architectural ambiguity, not simply high file counts
Use plan mode for both tasks, since any task touching production code benefits from an upfront planning phase regardless of complexity
Use direct execution for Task A to save time given the mechanical nature of the change, and plan mode for Task B to ensure the stack trace is fully understood before fixing
correct_answer: Use plan mode for Task A to scope the mechanical changes across all 50 files and validate the approach before execution; use direct execution for Task B since it is a well-understood, single-file fix
explanation: Plan mode is designed for large-scale, multi-file changes where validating the approach before execution prevents costly rework—even when the pattern itself is mechanical, touching 50 files benefits from an upfront scan to confirm consistency and catch edge cases across the codebase (option A). Direct execution is appropriate for Task B because it is a well-scoped, single-file fix with a clear stack trace, matching the guidance that simple, well-understood changes don't need the overhead of planning. Option B incorrectly implies that file count alone is irrelevant to the plan mode decision—multi-file modifications are explicitly called out as a trigger for plan mode. Option C over-applies plan mode to trivial fixes, adding unnecessary overhead. Option D reverses the appropriate approach for the two tasks.

text: You are integrating Claude Code into a GitHub Actions workflow to automatically review pull requests and post inline comments. The pipeline runs `claude -p "Review this diff for bugs and security issues"` and needs to feed structured findings into a script that posts PR comments programmatically. Additionally, when a PR receives new commits, the team wants to avoid Claude re-flagging issues it already reported in the previous review pass. What combination of configuration choices best supports these two requirements?
options: Use plain text output parsed with a custom regex script, and rerun the full review from scratch on every commit to ensure no issues are missed
Use `--output-format json` but omit prior findings from context, relying on Claude's training to avoid naturally repeating previous feedback it generated

Use `--output-format json` with a `--json-schema` to produce machine-parseable findings, and include the prior review's findings in the context on subsequent runs so Claude only reports new or unresolved issues
Switch to the Message Batches API for PR reviews to reduce cost, and compare each new batch result against the previous one using a diff tool to remove duplicates
correct_answer: Use `--output-format json` with a `--json-schema` to produce machine-parseable findings, and include the prior review's findings in the context on subsequent runs so Claude only reports new or unresolved issues
explanation: The `--output-format json` flag combined with `--json-schema` produces structured, machine-parseable output suitable for automated posting of inline PR comments, avoiding the fragility of parsing free-form text. For avoiding duplicate comments across review passes, the documented pattern is to include prior review findings in context when re-running reviews after new commits, explicitly instructing Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues (option C). Plain text with regex parsing (option A) is fragile and unnecessary given built-in structured output support. Omitting prior findings (option B) relies on an unsupported assumption that Claude will spontaneously avoid repeating feedback without being told about it. The Message Batches API (option D) is unsuitable here because PR review feedback is a blocking, latency-sensitive workflow, and batch processing has no guaranteed latency SLA.
